newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- U.S. Jan PPI seen up moderately.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- U.S. Jan PPI seen up moderately.

text.p: The U.S. Producer Price Index (PPI) probably edged up moderately in January, pointing to stable, but not decelerating, wholesale price trends, economists said.

In a Reuters poll, economists on average forecast a 0.3 percent rise in the overall PPI and a 0.2 percent increase in the so-called core PPI, the index minus its more volatile food and energy components.

Estimates for the January PPI rise ran as high as 0.6 percent at Nomura Securities International Inc and MCM International Inc, and as low as 0.1 percent at Daiwa Securities America Inc and JP Morgan and Co Inc.

Elliott Platt, managing director and head of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said he expected 0.2 percent gains in both the overall and core PPI. He characterized such rises as "obviously non-problematic."
Still, Platt said price trends at the intermediate and crude stages of production might not prove as beneficial for the credit markets as they had been previously.

"There seems to be a little updrift in some of the industrial materials prices -- in copper, zinc, nickel," he said. At the earlier production stages, the PPI has gone from negative readings to flattish readings, said Platt.
"The numbers (at the earlier stages) remain weak, but they are stabilizing as opposed to weakening further," he said.
Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America, expected the overall PPI to be up 0.1 percent and the core PPI to rise 0.2 percent.

"The information we look at suggests that food and energy prices dipped during the month and will actually be holding down the PPI," said Moran. "We look at the Agriculture Department's monthly survey of prices, and we look at various measures of gasoline prices, and all of that suggested that food and energy prices moved lower in January," he said.
Christopher Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, agreed that oil prices should have a beneficial effect on the PPI.
"The January PPI is due for better numbers just because the oil complex has come down," said Rupkey, who expects both the PPI and its core index to be up 0.2 percent.
The PPI rose 0.5 percent in December, while the core PPI rose just 0.1 percent.
"It's too early to see the PPI rise due to firmer commodity prices and more importantly, crude oil has collapsed here," said Rupkey.

"The latest (Federal Reserve) Beige Book said that the only price pressures evident anywhere were in oil "and now we're not even going to show that," said Rupkey. "Inflation is very quiet," he said. "There are some signs that wages are up and that could lead to price pressures down the road. Based on theory, prices should go up, but at the moment, we can't measure price pressure anywhere in the economy."

Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co Inc, also looked for subdued readings in both the overall and core January PPI. But he said that does not mean the credit markets can rest easy.

"You get back to the pace of activity out there (in the economy)," said Youngdahl. "That will keep people worried that the trends won't be as positive in the future as they have been. It's not like you're going to wake up and all of a sudden see 0.5 percent monthly gains, but you could get into a slowly upwardly grinding situation.
"The Fed wants to prevent that," said Youngdahl. "They want to be forward-looking and preemptive enough."
